content: Approximately 20% of the studies included in this analysis (n=7) focused exclusively on populations with the disease, resulting in a very high prevalence among the included studies. Due to the study design and the high prevalence, the quality of evidence was downgraded by one level. About half of the studies (n=18) concentrated on hereditary hemochromatosis, with most conducted in outpatient settings. There was unexplained heterogeneity observed, which may account for the multiple and highly variable diagnostic thresholds used. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed guidelines for using ferritin concentrations to assess iron status in individuals and populations. These guidelines were created with input from a steering group that included experts such as Dr. Francesco Branca, Director of the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, and Dr. Sebastien Cognat, Technical Officer for Capacity Assessment and Development. Other contributors included Dr. Nicola Magrini, Dr. Juan Pablo Peña-Rosas, Dr. Lisa M. Rogers, Dr. Abha Saxena, Dr. Amani Siyam, and Dr. Özge Tuncalp, among others, representing various fields such as nutrition, ethics, maternal health, and public health. The WHO Guideline Development Group included experts like Professor Salam Alkindi, specializing in hematology (sickle cell and thalassemia), and Dr. Gary Brittenham, an authority on iron metabolism and malaria. Other notable contributors were Professor Jonathan Gorstein, an expert in nutritional epidemiology, and Dr. Richard Hurrell, who focuses on biomarkers of nutrition and iron metabolism. The group also included Dr. Jianmeng Liu, specializing in genetics and micronutrient interventions, and Professor Petra Macaskill, an expert in biostatistics and systematic reviews. External resource persons, such as Dr. Rafael Flores-Ayala, Director of the International Micronutrient Malnutrition Prevention and Control Program, and Dr. Jahnavi Daru, a clinical researcher in women’s health, also contributed to the development of these guidelines. Their expertise spanned areas such as laboratory methods, public health nutrition, and clinical research. The systematic reviews conducted to inform these guidelines addressed several key questions. These included whether ferritin is an adequate marker of iron stores (both deficiency and overload), whether current ferritin cut-offs are accurate, and whether ferritin is a reliable marker for assessing the impact of iron interventions. The guidelines emphasize that ferritin concentrations can be influenced by subclinical inflammation, and adjustments may be necessary to accurately assess iron deficiency. For example, studies have shown that inflammation can elevate ferritin levels, potentially masking iron deficiency. The BRINDA (Biomarkers Reflecting Inflammation and Nutritional Determinants of Anemia) project has provided insights into adjusting ferritin concentrations to account for inflammation. Finally, the guidelines highlight the importance of determining population prevalence ranges for identifying public health problems related to iron deficiency. This involves using serum or plasma ferritin as a biomarker to assess the magnitude and distribution of iron deficiency across different countries and populations. The recommendations are based on systematic reviews and meta-analyses, ensuring that they are evidence-based and applicable to diverse settings.
